clue.text: Photographer mother of Erasmus?

explanation.surface: A photographer is cast as the mother of a famous humanist.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Brandt was a celebrated photographer; Sebastian Brant (also spelt Brandt) wrote The Ship of Fools, a forerunner of Erasmus's Praise of Folly, so figuratively its 'mother'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill Brandt was a leading twentieth-century camera artist, and the satirist Brant's book of fools spawned the Erasmian satire that followed it.

clue.text: People's poet put money on French ego on island

parts.note: to put money on something is to bet
je is French for I, the ego
the Isle of Man, often just Man in crosswords

explanation.surface: A gambler stakes cash on a French self living on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link placing the island after the rest in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Betjeman, Poet Laureate, was hugely popular with ordinary readers, a poet of the people.

clue.text: Shelley's demon is sadly on the hill

parts.note: alas is an exclamation expressing sadness
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Shelley's demon is mournfully perched on a hilltop.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley's poem Alastor, or the Spirit of Solitude, names an avenging spirit, a demon of solitude.

clue.text: Like Defoe, he does not conform

definitions.text: Like Defoe, he does not conform

parts.words: Like Defoe, he does not conform
parts.note: Defoe belonged to the Protestant Nonconformists outside the Church of England; the clue describes such a person

explanation.surface: Defoe is presented as a typical rebel against convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nonconformist Protestant who refused the Church of England was called by this name, as Defoe was.

clue.text: Come to earth after little speedster suggests late novelist

indicators.note: after places the landing word behind the little car word

parts.note: a go-cart is a small fast racing car
to land is to come down to the ground

explanation.surface: A small fast car touching down hints at a dead writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbara Cartland, the prolific romantic novelist, died in 2000.

clue.text: King at southern battle scene known to advise Belgian investigator

parts.note: Arthur was the legendary British king
the Battle of Hastings, 1066, took place in the south of England

explanation.surface: A king at a southern battlefield is said to counsel a Belgian sleuth.
explanation.walkthrough: The Belgian investigator is Agatha Christie's Hercule Poirot, whose companion and sounding-board is Captain Hastings.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Hastings is Poirot's friend and narrator, who offers the detective his (usually wrong) counsel.

clue.text: Unspoken, like the greater part of Roman historian

indicators.note: the greater part means most of the word is kept, its final letters dropped

parts.note: Tacitus was the Roman historian of the Annals

explanation.surface: Something silent is compared to most of a Roman writer.
explanation.walkthrough: TACITUS loses its last two letters, US. The historian's name itself means 'silent' in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means understood without being said aloud, implied rather than stated.

clue.text: Quasi an unusual theologian

indicators.note: unusual tells us the letters of the preceding words appear in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A theologian is described as almost peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Aquinas was the great medieval scholastic thinker of the Church.

clue.text: In this case I've underwritten a little bit on the way up

indicators.note: underwritten places the words for I've beneath the other piece in the column
in a down clue, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a tad is a small amount
the clue word itself, minus apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone insures a small item heading upward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the way up' turns TAD into DAT; 'underwritten' puts IVE below it.
explanation.definitionFit: The dative is a grammatical case, used for indirect objects.

clue.text: We launch Gaunt's new version of world philosophy

indicators.note: a new version of the words means their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, including the s

explanation.surface: Someone promotes a fresh edition of Gaunt's view of life.
explanation.definitionFit: The German term means an overall view of the world, a comprehensive outlook on life.

clue.text: Shakespearian doxy removed from publication

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean strumpet is taken out of print.
explanation.definitionFit: Doll Tearsheet is the prostitute in Henry IV Part 2; a tear sheet is a page torn out of a magazine or newspaper.

clue.text: That of love, once attributed to Chaucer, appropriately in rhyme-royal

definitions.text: That of love, once attributed to Chaucer, appropriately in rhyme-royal

parts.words: That of love, once attributed to Chaucer, appropriately in rhyme-royal
parts.note: a fifteenth-century allegorical poem about the tribunal of the god of love, long wrongly ascribed to Chaucer

explanation.surface: A poem about love, formerly credited to Chaucer, is written in a stanza named for royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: The Court of Love is in rhyme royal, apt because a royal court suits a regal stanza form.
explanation.definitionFit: A royal court is the household of a monarch, hence the pun on rhyme royal.

clue.text: "Hesperus —s thy light, / Goddess, excellently bright." (Ben Jonson)

definitions.text: "Hesperus —s thy light, / Goddess, excellently bright." (Ben Jonson)

parts.words: "Hesperus —s thy light, / Goddess, excellently bright." (Ben Jonson)
parts.note: the missing verb comes from Jonson's Hymn to Diana in Cynthia's Revels, where the evening star begs the moon

explanation.surface: A line from Ben Jonson's hymn to the moon goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: The evening star beseeches the moon to shine; to beseech is to beg earnestly.

clue.text: His play was overheard

parts.note: the playwright and actor wrote a 1981 comedy with this very word as its title

explanation.surface: Someone's play was eavesdropped on.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Ustinov's play Overheard (1981): 'overheard' is the title, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Peter Ustinov, actor and dramatist, wrote the comedy Overheard.

clue.text: Evil demon discerned in tea-leaf ritual ()

indicators.note: discerned in means the letters can be seen inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller spots a fiend in the tea leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: An afrit is a powerful malevolent spirit of Arabian mythology.

clue.text: Nothing adequately describes such disbelief

parts.note: the Latin word for nothing is the root of the name of this creed of total rejection, so 'nothing' literally describes it

explanation.surface: Words fail to capture such scepticism.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine rejecting all values and beliefs is named from Latin nihil, meaning nothing.

clue.text: Eighteenth-century mock epic drama with big part for a maid

definitions.text: drama with big part for a maid

explanation.surface: A satirical poem and a play both feature a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Voltaire's mock epic about Joan of Arc; in Henry VI Part 1 Joan appears as 'Joan la Pucelle', French for the maid.
explanation.definitionFit: Voltaire's burlesque poem bears Joan of Arc's French title, the Maid, which is also her name in Shakespeare's Henry VI.

clue.text: Describes group of three books, seminal — isn't copy, anyway

definitions.text: Describes group of three books, seminal

indicators.note: anyway, read as any way, says the letters may be set in any order

explanation.surface: A trio of foundational books is described, none merely imitative.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew, Mark and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels because they share a common view.

clue.text: High sheriff of Durham's Cockney grocer

definitions.text: High sheriff of Durham's Cockney grocer

parts.words: High sheriff of Durham's Cockney grocer
parts.note: R. S. Surtees, once High Sheriff of Durham, created a sporting London tradesman who rides to hounds

explanation.surface: A Durham official's working-class London shopkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: Surtees, who served as Durham's High Sheriff, invented the fox-hunting London merchant John Jorrocks.

clue.text: Frank Norris's sea creature, dear to Dodie Smith

explanation.surface: A novelist's marine animal is beloved by a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank Norris wrote the novel The Octopus (1901); Dodie Smith wrote the play Dear Octopus (1938).
explanation.definitionFit: Norris named his novel after the eight-armed mollusc, and Smith's play title calls the family that same creature.

clue.text: Shakespeare's Cesario really a sort of —

definitions.text: Shakespeare's Cesario really a sort of —

parts.words: Shakespeare's Cesario really a sort of —
parts.note: in Twelfth Night Cesario is the disguised Viola, and a viola is a garden flower of a related kind

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's page boy is really effeminate.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a slur on the cross-dressed page; really Viola is a flower of the violet family.
explanation.definitionFit: Violas and the garden flowers with velvety faces are close relatives in the genus Viola.

clue.text: Novelist makes a point to first-class evangelist

parts.note: N, north, is a compass point
A1 means first-class, with the 1 written as I
St Paul was the great missionary preacher

explanation.surface: A writer makes a point to a top-rate preacher.
explanation.definitionFit: V. S. Naipaul was the Nobel-winning Trinidad-born writer of fiction.

clue.text: "Thirty-six were cast for death, and only one was '-'"(Henry Mayhew)

definitions.text: "Thirty-six were cast for death, and only one was '-'"(Henry Mayhew)

parts.words: "Thirty-six were cast for death, and only one was '-'"(Henry Mayhew)
parts.note: Mayhew is speaking of condemned prisoners, only one of whom was actually executed; the slang word for hanged fills the gap

explanation.surface: A Victorian journalist on the death sentences actually carried out.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for executed, especially by hanging, is to have been killed off by the hangman.

clue.text: Triumvir's wife as seen by Jilly Cooper

explanation.surface: Mark Antony's spouse is viewed through a popular novelist's eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: Octavian's sister married the triumvir Mark Antony; Jilly Cooper wrote a romantic novel with her name as its title.

clue.text: Part Slav, arrogant polymath praised by Cicero and Quintilian

definitions.text: polymath praised by Cicero and Quintilian

indicators.note: part signals that a portion of the following words makes up the answer

explanation.surface: A partly Slavic, haughty scholar is praised by Roman orators.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Terentius Varro was the most learned Roman scholar, writing on every subject.

clue.text: Would-be seducer who received reportedly posthumous reward

definitions.text: Would-be seducer who received reportedly posthumous reward

parts.words: Would-be seducer who received reportedly posthumous reward
parts.note: in Cymbeline the villain who tries to seduce Imogen is finally pardoned by her husband Posthumus, a name sounding like the word posthumous

explanation.surface: A failed seducer gets a reward after death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'posthumous' puns on Posthumus Leonatus, who spares the villain at the end of Cymbeline.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian in Cymbeline wagers he can seduce Imogen and fails.

clue.text: War artists whose patrons presumably called the tune

definitions.text: War artists whose patrons presumably called the tune

parts.words: War artists whose patrons presumably called the tune
parts.note: John ... was an official Second World War artist, and the proverb says he who pays this musician calls the tune

explanation.surface: Wartime painters whose sponsors dictated the subjects.
explanation.definitionFit: John Piper painted bomb-damaged buildings as a war artist, and the proverb names a bagpipe player.

clue.text: "Van Dyck was so —— as to dispute with her on the price of her picture" (Horace Walpole)

definitions.text: "Van Dyck was so —— as to dispute with her on the price of her picture" (Horace Walpole)

parts.words: "Van Dyck was so —— as to dispute with her on the price of her picture" (Horace Walpole)
parts.note: Walpole means the painter was discourteous to a lady in haggling with her

explanation.surface: Walpole on a painter haggling with a lady sitter.
explanation.definitionFit: Haggling with a lady was discourteous, lacking chivalry toward women.

clue.text: Remove Elizabethan dramatist, or some beavers?

definitions.text: Remove Elizabethan dramatist, or some beavers?

parts.words: Remove Elizabethan dramatist, or some beavers?
parts.note: Thomas Lodge was an Elizabethan playwright and a beaver's home is a lodge, so evicting either is jokingly described

explanation.surface: Get rid of an old playwright, or of beavers.
explanation.definitionFit: To dislodge is to force out of a position, here punningly removing a Lodge.

clue.text: Naturalized poet gets the Spanish into coalition

indicators.note: into places the Spanish article inside the coalition word

parts.note: a bloc is an alliance of parties or nations
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A poet who became a citizen joins a political alliance in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc, French-born, became a British subject in 1902.
